newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal communist-led alliance to aid private sector.
newsitem.headline: Nepal communist-led alliance to aid private sector.

text.p: Nepal's King Birendra pledged on Wednesday that the Himalayan kingdom's communist-dominated coalition government would nurture its fledgling private sector.

"My government will gradually reduce its role in the public corporations and encourage the private sector to participate," the 51-year old monarch, Nepal's constitutional head, said in his traditional address to the Nepali parliament.
"Concrete policies will be adopted for the development of the private sector and creation of a favourable atmosphere for investment," the king said without elaborating.

Nepal, where a multi-party democracy was established through a popular movement seven years ago, opened up to a market economy in 1992 and began welcoming private and foreign investment to one the world's 10 poorest countries.
More than a dozen state-run enterprises were sold to the private sector as part of the reforms programme, which slowed during nine months of communist rule in 1994 and 1995.

The king's address, prepared by the government, spells out the policies and programmes of Prime Minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand, who assumed office in March at the head of a coalition in which the communists are dominant partners.
Parliament officials said the royal address would be debated in parliament later this week. A subsequent vote of thanks by parliament would constitute approval of the policies.
A similar vote failed to pass three years ago when some dissident members of the ruling Nepali Congress party abstained, forcing the government to step down and order mid-term elections.
The king said Chand would implement a water-sharing treaty signed last year with India, which resolves a 10-year-old dispute with New Delhi giving Nepal more benefits from two old dams.

The treaty, which defines terms for the construction of a multi-billion dollar dam on the Mahakali river on Nepal's western borders with India, was made effective in June when Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral made an official visit to Kathmandu.
Nepal and India will equally share the 6,000 megawatts of hydroelectric power to be produced by the project.
